hook: The owner of a taco truck writes down how many tacos she sells at each price she tries. A list of numbers is hard to read at a glance, but put the same numbers on a graph and the pattern jumps out: the lower the price, the more tacos go out the window. Every graph in this course starts with two labeled axes and points read from them.

figure.caption: Three rows of the taco table plotted as ordered pairs (tacos sold, price). Each point has dashed lines to both axes. The points fall to the right: an inverse relationship. Invented data for practice.

chain.cause: You pick the two variables to compare
chain.effect: one goes on the horizontal axis and one on the vertical axis, each labeled with its name and units

chain.cause: Each row of a table gives one value of each variable
chain.effect: it becomes one ordered pair (horizontal value, vertical value)
the points show a pattern you can read at a glance

chain.cause: The points rise to the right or fall to the right
chain.effect: the variables have a direct or an inverse relationship

ideas: The horizontal axis (x-axis) runs left to right; the vertical axis (y-axis) runs up. On a market graph, quantity goes across and price goes up.
An ordered pair (x, y) names one point: first the horizontal value, then the vertical value.
To read a point, drop a line straight down to the horizontal axis and across to the vertical axis.
A direct relationship: both variables rise together, so the points rise to the right. An inverse relationship: one rises as the other falls, so the points fall to the right.
Label both axes every time. An unlabeled axis loses the graph point on the exam.

misconception.wrong: The ordered pair (80, 3) on a price and quantity graph means a price of \$80 and 80 tacos is not on the graph.
misconception.right: The first number is always the horizontal value. With quantity across and price up, (80, 3) means 80 tacos at a price of \$3.

summary: A graph has two labeled axes: the horizontal axis (x) and the vertical axis (y). On a market graph, quantity goes on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical. Each row of a table becomes an ordered pair (horizontal value, vertical value), and you read a point by dropping lines to both axes. Points that rise to the right show a direct relationship; points that fall to the right show an inverse one.
